newsitem.title: USA: Budget clears New Jersey legislature.
newsitem.headline: Budget clears New Jersey legislature.

text.p: A $16.8 billion, election- year budget cleared both chambers of the New Jersey Legislature Thursday but not without a protracted partisan debate.
Gov. Christie Whitman plans a signing ceremony for Friday.
In a year with all 40 Senate seats and 80 in the Assembly on the Nov. 4 ballot, the opposition was pro forma. The budget was full of special items to attract support.

The budget has grown by $400 million since she introduced it in January, Assemblyman Joseph Roberts Jr., D-Camden, pointed out. "This may be the most decorated Christmas tree to ever grace our presence," he said.

Among the new spending is $246 million to satisfy the Supreme Court order to increase state aid to the 28 poorest school districts; $55 million in high tech grants for higher education plus $30 million for college salaries, and $18 million to increase the state's child protection staff.
Several Democrats recalled that two proposals were rejected -- $100 million to pay mostly urban hospitals for charity care and $55 million to fund a child-care tax credit.
Roberts complained that the $40 million in special items was unprecedented both for its size and for favoring Republican districts.
The extra spending was made possible by two developments.
-- Whitman's plan to sell $2.75 billion in pension bonds, enabling the state to skip $590 million in contributions to the four funds it runs.
-- An unanticipated bounty of tax revenue, estimated to exceed budget projections by $500 million.
"The tough vote was not on the budget but on the pension bond sale two weeks ago," said state Sen. Joseph Kyrillos, R-Middlesex. "Once that was decided, the rest was easy."
That issue has not been finally resolved, even though the bonds were sold in record time earlier this week.

A Democratic challenge to the bond sale -- rebuffed by a Superior Court judge and an appeals court panel -- has been appealed to the state Supreme Court. The lower courts rejected the contention that the state Constitution requires a referendum vote on the bond issue.

The bonds are being sold by the state Economic Development Authority, under contract to the state Treasurer to have the state pay them off. The courts have ruled that the deal was structured to avoid direct state debt, so a popular vote was not needed.
